html:
The Sushruta Samhita is a Sanskrit book of medicine and surgery, one of the founding texts of Ayurveda. It is named after Sushruta, a physician said to have taught at Varanasi. Its oldest layer may go back to the middle of the first millennium BCE; the text as it survives was finished by about 500 CE.

It is the most detailed account of surgery to survive from the ancient world. It describes:

  • more than 120 surgical instruments, many named after the animal whose beak or jaw they look like;
  • about 300 operations, among them removing a cataract by pushing the lens aside with a needle, cutting for bladder stones and setting bones;
  • rebuilding a cut-off nose with a flap of skin from the cheek;
  • training: students practised cuts on gourds and stitches on cloth, and studied the body by soaking a corpse in water.

Its partner text, the Charaka Samhita, deals with general medicine: diet, drugs and the balance of the body's three humours.

The book was translated into Arabic in Baghdad in the 8th century. The Indian nose operation was reported in a London magazine in 1794 and started modern plastic surgery in Europe.
